> Abstract:We revisit the problem of defining natural torsion and curvature tensors for generalised connections and of using them to reconstruct the effective action for the massless modes of the closed string from generalised geometry. The starting point is the description of a Courant algebroid as a differential graded (dg) symplectic manifold. A systematic procedure for split dg manifolds singles out a generalised Lie bracket as part of a larger Lie 2-algebroid structure, with the right properties to unambiguously define torsion and Riemann curvature tensors together with their corresponding Bianchi identities. This framework eliminates the structural circularity and ambiguity problems of previous approaches in the literature. We show that a unique generalised metric compatible generalised connection with fixed (con)torsion exists for any choice of ordinary connection that splits the dg manifold, while at the same time all Lie 2-algebroids obtained in this way are equivalent up to $L_{\infty}$ quasi-isomorphisms. For a given Lie 2-algebroid we demonstrate that the unique compatible generalised connection reproduces the effective closed string action from a geometric action based on the new generalised Ricci tensor upon making a canonical choice of torsion.

# Sunflower-Free Uniform Families: Recursive Constructions and Explicit Bounds

Edward Axante, Cristian Budala, David Chitic, Bogdan Dumitru, Mihai Nacu


## Abstract

Let $f(w,k)$ be the maximum size of a $w$-uniform family containing no sunflower with $k$ petals. We introduce a recursive construction for sunflower-free families and use it to obtain a general lower bound on the exponential growth rate of $f(w,k)$. We also prove a general upper bound for $3$-uniform families with at least four petals. Our results give $39\le f(3,4)\le49$, $f(3,5)\le146$, $153\le f(3,6)\le255$, $259\le f(3,7)\le474$, and $54\le f(4,3)\le83$. In addition, we prove that the maximum size of an intersecting $4$-uniform family containing no sunflower with three petals is $27$. The upper bounds $49$ and $83$ are computer-assisted. The finite lower bounds come from explicit constructions.

Chris — this one is worth a serious read. The Koszul-style uniqueness result and the Bianchi identities are the real substance, and in this combination they are new. ## What was actually shown

The manuscript claims a computer-assisted exclusion of 69-member three-sunflower-free four-uniform families, giving 54 <= M(4,3) <= 68. It improves the upper bound 83 in Axante et al., arXiv:2609.06175v1, Theorem 6.9. The classical lower construction is reproduced, not claimed as new. The proof combines their intersecting-family bound 27, structural point-link reductions, Jin's graph-homomorphism theorem, exact certificates and finite exhaustive checks. A local cap of 61 requires a complete R16 point-link and is not a global bound. Cardinality 68 is not excluded, the exact value is not determined, and the general sunflower conjecture (Erdős #20) remains open.

## What the AI did

The author reports using OpenAI Sol 5.6, Astra 6, Pro 6 and Sol 6.1. As disclosed in the manuscript, generative AI tools assisted proof development, software preparation and manuscript review. The named human author retains responsibility for the claims. The model names are the author's disclosure for this submission; the manuscript does not identify versions or attribute individual lemmas to particular models. Author-side AI reviews are not independent specialist verification.

## Verification

No independent mathematician has checked this yet. Checked by this site on 15 October 2026: the aiXiv v1 record and PDF open (CC BY, content-hashed, not withdrawn), the pinned GitHub commit 90c03c7 exists, and the manuscript's AI disclosure and Theorem 1.1 were read. Axante et al., arXiv:2609.06175v1 (still the only version), was read for Table 1, Proposition 6.7 (the imported bound 27) and Theorem 6.9 (54 <= f(4,3) <= 83). A separate script written here confirmed that the 54-member construction has no sunflower among its 24,804 triples, that no further four-set on its 18 points can be added, and that a graph with no three-edge sunflower has at most six edges (Lemma 3.1, on seven vertices). The companion's 42 finite suites (about 53 minutes) were not re-run here, nor was the imported exhaustive computation behind the bound 27, itself an AI-assisted preprint result from September 2026. The upper bound 68 rests on those computations and the written reductions; the author-side AI reviews are not independent.

We introduce an operational framework for heat-exchange statistics between a quantum field and an Unruh-DeWitt detector in Minkowski spacetime. Using an interferometric protocol, we define the characteristic function of heat without projective measurements, consistently with relativistic causality. We derive perturbative expressions for this function and the heat distribution. In the vacuum, the statistics coincides with the low-intensity expansion of a unidirectional Poisson law, while for Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (KMS) states it has a bidirectional Poisson structure up to second order in perturbation theory. These results provide a consistent framework for heat statistics in relativistic quantum field theory and clarify the emergence of fluctuation relations.

## What was actually shown

The manuscript claims a computer-assisted exclusion of 69-member three-sunflower-free four-uniform families, giving 54 <= M(4,3) <= 68. It improves the upper bound 83 in Axante et al., arXiv:2609.06175v1, Theorem 6.9. The classical lower construction is reproduced, not claimed as new. The proof combines their intersecting-family bound 27, structural point-link reductions, Jin's graph-homomorphism theorem, exact certificates and finite exhaustive checks. A local cap of 61 requires a complete R16 point-link and is not a global bound. Cardinality 68 is not excluded, the exact value is not determined, and the general sunflower conjecture (Erdős #20) remains open.

## What the AI did

The author reports using OpenAI Sol 5.6, Astra 6, Pro 6 and Sol 6.1. As disclosed in the manuscript, generative AI tools assisted proof development, software preparation and manuscript review. The named human author retains responsibility for the claims. The model names are the author's disclosure for this submission; the manuscript does not identify versions or attribute individual lemmas to particular models. Author-side AI reviews are not independent specialist verification.

## Verification

No independent mathematician has checked this yet. Checked by this site on 15 October 2026: the aiXiv v1 record and PDF open (CC BY, content-hashed, not withdrawn), the pinned GitHub commit 90c03c7 exists, and the manuscript's AI disclosure and Theorem 1.1 were read. Axante et al., arXiv:2609.06175v1 (still the only version), was read for Table 1, Proposition 6.7 (the imported bound 27) and Theorem 6.9 (54 <= f(4,3) <= 83). A separate script written here confirmed that the 54-member construction has no sunflower among its 24,804 triples, that no further four-set on its 18 points can be added, and that a graph with no three-edge sunflower has at most six edges (Lemma 3.1, on seven vertices). The companion's 42 finite suites (about 53 minutes) were not re-run here, nor was the imported exhaustive computation behind the bound 27, itself an AI-assisted preprint result from September 2026. The upper bound 68 rests on those computations and the written reductions; the author-side AI reviews are not independent.

As I mentioned in the comments, this is not an easier question. Indeed, one can start with a maximal $t$-sunflower-free collection in uniformity $k-1$, and then add a unique "dummy element" to each edge in this construction. Thus, your problem has a bound of $\exp(O_t(k))$ if and only if the original Erdos-Rado problem has a bound of $\exp(O_t(k))$.

Here's an attempt to propose a new question in the spirit you intended:

> Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a $k$-uniform $t$-sunflower-free family. Is there some vertex that is contained in at least $c_t^k|\mathcal{H}|$ of the edges (where $c_t>0$ is some absolute constant)?

EDIT: my question is also silly. If no element is contained by a $(1/tk)$-fraction of the edges from $\mathcal{H}$, then we can greedily find $t$ disjoint sets.

L26: > Abstract: Let $M(4,3)$ be the maximum size of a finite simple family of four-element sets containing no three distinct members whose pairwise intersections are equal. The empty intersection is included in the forbidden configurations. We give a computer-assisted exclusion of families of size $69$, giving the bound $54\le M(4,3)\le 68$. The argument combines an imported bound of $27$ for intersecting families, structural analysis of point-links, exact trace constraints and finite exhaustions.
L27: The proof is organized at the cardinality $69$. A cap on families containing a complete $R16$ point-link provides a shorter final contradiction. We make the imported results, computational lemma contracts and remaining verification limits explicit. The lower construction is classical. Neither exclusion of size $68$ nor optimality of the lower construction is claimed.

Structural point-link analysis and exact trace constraints reduce the maximum-degree possibilities. Jin's strict graph-homomorphism theorem, in the formulation of Nikiforov's Theorem A, then supplies a fibre decomposition. L54: # Sunflower-Free Uniform Families: Recursive Constructions and Explicit Bounds
L55: 
L56: Edward Axante ^{†}^{†}thanks: Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, University of Bucharest, Romania.    Cristian Budala^{1}^{1}footnotemark: 1    David Chitic^{1}^{1}footnotemark: 1    Bogdan Dumitru^{1}^{1}footnotemark: 1    and Mihai Nacu^{1}^{1}footnotemark: 1
L57: ###### Abstract
L58: Let $f(w,k)$ be the maximum size of a $w$-uniform family containing no sunflower with $k$ petals. We introduce a recursive construction for sunflower-free families and use it to obtain a general lower bound on the exponential growth rate of $f(w,k)$. We also prove a general upper bound for $3$-uniform families with at least four petals. Our results give $39\leq f(3,4)\leq 49$, $f(3,5)\leq 146$, $153\leq f(3,6)\leq 255$, $259\leq f(3,7)\leq 474$, and $54\leq f(4,3)\leq 83$.
L59: In addition, we prove that the maximum size of an intersecting $4$-uniform family containing no sunflower with three petals is $27$. The upper bounds $49$ and $83$ are computer-assisted. The finite lower bounds come from explicit constructions.
L60: ## 1 Introduction
L61: A sunflower with $k$ petals, or $k$-sunflower, is a collection of $k$ distinct sets whose pairwise intersections are equal. Their common intersection is called the core and may be empty. Let $f(w,k)$ denote the maximum size of a family of distinct $w$-element sets containing no $k$-sunflower. The sunflower conjecture of Erdős and Rado asks whether, for every fixed $k$, there is a constant $C_{k}$ such that $f(w,k)\leq C_{k}^{w}$ for every $w$ [【42†11】].
L62: Alweiss, Lovett, Wu, and Zhang substantially improved the classical upper bound [【43†6】], and Bell, Chueluecha, and Warnke subsequently proved $f(w,k)\leq(Ck\log w)^{w}$ for an absolute constant $C$ and all $w,k\geq 2$ [【44†7】].
L63: Our lower-bound arguments keep track not only of the absence of sunflowers but also of the maximum number of pairwise disjoint members. Controlling this matching number rules out sunflowers with empty core. Within this framework, we construct larger sunflower-free families from smaller ones by attaching subsets of an auxiliary set. The resulting recurrence leads to an explicit general lower bound on the exponential growth rate of $f(w,k)$.
L64: An alternative construction based on a bounded-degree auxiliary graph is included in the appendix.
L65: Abbott and Hanson introduced the study of sunflower-free families with a bounded matching number and showed how families on disjoint ground sets can be combined to obtain lower bounds for $f(w,k)$ [【45†4】]. For three petals, our main recurrence follows from a multiplication theorem of Abbott and Exoo [【46†5】]. We extend this recurrence to arbitrary numbers of petals and all admissible matching-number bounds.
L66: To our knowledge, this recurrence, the alternative recurrence in the appendix, and the resulting exponential lower bound are new. Abbott and Hanson raised the problem of proving recurrences for $\psi$ and reported no success [【45†4】, p. 11]. The closest prior forms are an additive recurrence of Abbott and Exoo for three petals [【46†5】, Theorem 3] and an edge-attachment product of Frankl and Wang [【47†13】, Proposition 2.1].
L67: For $k-1\geq 3w(m-1)$, Frankl and Wang determine $\psi(w,k,m)$ exactly [【47†13】, Theorem 1.11]; the bounds proved here concern fixed $k$ and growing $w$, outside that regime.
L68: For upper bounds on families of triples, we begin with a largest collection of pairwise disjoint triples and classify all other members by how they intersect its union. This reduces the problem to degree and matching bounds for ordinary graphs, to which we apply the theorem of Chvátal and Hanson [【48†9】]. The resulting argument gives a general upper bound for $f(3,k)$ when $k\geq 4$. Separate finite analyses sharpen the result for $f(3,4)$ and give the upper bound for $f(4,3)$.
L69: 【49†Table 1】 compares the numerical bounds obtained in this paper with previously published bounds. The two published endpoints shown for $f(3,7)$ follow from Proposition 2.1 and Theorem 1.14, respectively, of Frankl and Wang [【47†13】].
L70: Table 1: Published comparisons and bounds proved in this paper.

L72: --- | --- | ---
L73: $f(3,4)$  | $38$ [【46†5】] $\leq f(3,4)$  | $\leq$  | $69$ [【50†3】]  | $39\leq f(3,4)$  | $\leq$  | $49$
L74: $f(3,5)$  | $f(3,5)$  | $\leq$  | $180$ [【50†3】]  | $f(3,5)$  | $\leq$  | $146$
L75: $f(3,6)$  | $146$ [【46†5】] $\leq f(3,6)$  | $\leq$  | $305$ [【50†3】]  | $153\leq f(3,6)$  | $\leq$  | $255$
L76: $f(3,7)$  | $252\leq f(3,7)$  | $\leq$  | $498$ [【47†13】]  | $259\leq f(3,7)$  | $\leq$  | $474$
L77: $f(4,3)$  | $54$ [【45†4】] $\leq f(4,3)$  | $\leq$  | $142$ [【50†3】]  | $54\leq f(4,3)$  | $\leq$  | $83$
L78: The upper bounds $f(3,4)\leq 49$ and $f(4,3)\leq 83$ are computer-assisted and follow from exhaustive finite enumerations. The lower bounds $f(3,4)\geq 39$ and $f(3,7)\geq 259$ are established by explicit finite families. We also determine exactly the maximum size of an intersecting $4$-uniform family containing no $3$-sunflower: it is $27$.
L79: The main combinatorial arguments of 【7†sections 2】, 【12†3】 and 【16†4】, the appendix capacity recurrence, and every explicit finite lower-bound witness have additionally been formalised and machine-checked in the Lean 4 proof assistant (【38†section 8】).^{1}^{1} 1 Code, data, and the Lean development are available at 【51†https://github.com/bogdan27182/sunflower-paper†github.com】.
L80: ## 2 Notation and preliminary facts
L81: 
L82: This section fixes the notation and records the basic facts used in the paper. We introduce links and the matching-constrained extremal quantity, determine the cases of uniformity one and two, and recall the product inequality used to define the exponential growth rate.
L83: ### 2.1 Set families
L84: 
L85: All set families in this paper are finite and have distinct members. All graphs are finite and simple. For a finite set $X$, write
L86: 
L87:  | $$\binom{X}{w}=\{A\subseteq X:|A|=w\}.$$  |
L88: 
L89: A family $\mathcal{F}$ is $w$-uniform if $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\binom{X}{w}$ for some finite set $X$. Its support is
L90: 
L91:  | $$\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{F})=\bigcup_{F\in\mathcal{F}}F.$$  |
L92: 
L93: If distinct sets $A_{1},\ldots,A_{k}$ satisfy
L94: 
L95:  | $$A_{i}\cap A_{j}=C\qquad(1\leq i<j\leq k),$$  |
L96: then they form a $k$-sunflower with core $C$. The core may be empty. The sets $A_{i}\setminus C$ are its petals. For $w\geq 1$ and $k\geq 2$, define
L97: 
L98:  | $$f(w,k)=\max\bigl\{|\mathcal{F}|:\mathcal{F}\text{ is $w$-uniform and contains no
L99: $k$-sunflower}\bigr\}.$$  |  | (2.1)
L100: 
L101: The Erdős–Rado sunflower lemma makes this maximum finite [【42†11】].
L102: ###### Lemma 2.1 (Occurrence rule).
L103: 
L104: Let $A_{1},\ldots,A_{k}$ form a sunflower. Every point in $A_{1}\cup\cdots\cup A_{k}$ belongs to exactly one member or to all $k$ members.
L105: 
L106: ###### Proof.
L107: 
L108: Suppose that a point belongs to two members. It then belongs to their intersection, which is the core. Hence it belongs to every member. ∎
L109: 
L110: The core of a sunflower of distinct $w$-element sets has size at most $w-1$. In particular, the possible core sizes for a sunflower of triples are zero, one, and two.
L111: ### 2.2 Matchings, degrees, and links
L112: 
L113: A matching in a family is a subfamily of pairwise disjoint members. The matching number $\nu(\mathcal{F})$ is the largest size of a matching in $\mathcal{F}$. A family is intersecting if every two distinct members meet. Equivalently, $\nu(\mathcal{F})\leq 1$. Since a matching of size $k$ is a $k$-sunflower with empty core, every $k$-sunflower-free family satisfies
L114: 
L115:  | $$\nu(\mathcal{F})\leq k-1.$$  |  | (2.2)
L116: 
L117: For $m\geq 2$, define
L118:  | $$\psi(w,k,m)=\max\bigl\{|\mathcal{F}|:\mathcal{F}\text{ is $w$-uniform, contains no
L119: $k$-sunflower, and }\nu(\mathcal{F})\leq m-1\bigr\}.$$  |  | (2.3)
L120: 
L121: This matching-constrained quantity was introduced by Abbott and Hanson [【45†4】]. In particular, $\psi(w,k,2)$ is the maximum over intersecting $w$-uniform families without a $k$-sunflower, while $\psi(w,k,k)=f(w,k)$.
L122: 
L123: For a set $S$, define its degree in $\mathcal{F}$ by
L124: 
L125:  | $$d_{\mathcal{F}}(S)=|\{F\in\mathcal{F}:S\subseteq F\}|.$$  |

# An upper bound for three-sunflower-free families of four-element sets

Oleksiy Babanskyy

[Read the paper](paper/Four-Uniform-Three-Sunflower-Bound.pdf) ·
[Reproduce the computations](REPRODUCE.md) ·
[Mathematical dependencies](proof/DEPENDENCIES.md)

The manuscript gives a computer-assisted upper bound of **68** for the
maximum size M(4,3) of a finite simple four-uniform family containing no three
distinct sets with equal pairwise intersections. The empty kernel is included
among the forbidden configurations. Together with the classical 54-member
construction, this gives

    54 ≤ M(4,3) ≤ 68.

Equivalently, every finite simple four-uniform family of at least 69 sets contains a three-sunflower.
The first forcing threshold is M(4,3)+1. Exclusion of size 68, optimality of
54, record priority and a solution of the general sunflower conjecture are
not claimed.

The proof imports the intersecting-family upper bound 27 from Proposition
6.7 of Axante et al., arXiv:2609.06175v1, and uses Jin’s strict graph
homomorphism theorem as stated in Nikiforov’s Theorem A. The companion does
not re-execute the external H27 calculation. Its finite route includes nine
preliminary blocks, the separate C5 obstruction, both degree-17 transport
cores and the terminal contradiction at 69. Finite comparisons use exact
integer or rational arithmetic; the paper and linked proofs establish the
reductions connecting them to the theorem.

## Verify

Python 3.10 or newer and its standard library suffice. From the repository
root:

    python -B scripts/check_repository.py
    python -B scripts/run_checks.py --mode quick --output build/quick
    python -B scripts/run_checks.py --mode complete --output build/complete

Each run requires a new output directory. The wrapper creates an isolated
computational copy and saves receipts under its output directory. Quick
checks report `QUICK_PARTIAL_PASS`; they are partial. Only the complete route
checks all 42 named finite suites, normally and with Python -O, and reports
`COMPLETE_COMPANION_PASS`. See [REPRODUCE.md](REPRODUCE.md) for receipt
checking, paper builds, failure controls and the qualified historical
verification record. A computational PASS does not formalize the written
proof or constitute external human reproduction.

| [proof/DEPENDENCIES.md](proof/DEPENDENCIES.md) | Logical dependencies and links to written reductions |

# Sunflower-Free Uniform Families: Recursive Constructions and Explicit Bounds

This repository contains the supplementary material for the paper: explicit
witnesses, finite-enumeration source, archived search ledgers, independently
checked SAT certificates, and the Lean 4 formalisation of the paper's
combinatorial results.

## Release status

The computational artifact set is complete and passes its checks.  In
particular, the four authenticated cross-search ledgers for the proof of
`f(3,4) <= 49` are included and reproduce the published totals.  The `lean/`
directory is still a placeholder in this working copy and must be replaced by
the formalisation in `../lean` before the final manifest is generated.

The preferred project license must still be supplied before publication.

## Contents

| Result | Public artifact | Verification |
|---|---|---|
| `f(3,4) <= 49` | `artifacts/f34_upper_49` | rooted blocks, routing covers, profiles, cross-search ledgers |
| Proposition 6.1 | `artifacts/f43_upper_83/triple_inputs` | 16 independently checked CNF/DRAT certificates |
| intersecting 4-uniform maximum 27 | `artifacts/f43_upper_83/intersecting_27` | archived 11,720-root exhaustive search |
| `f(3,7) >= 259` | `artifacts/f37_lower_259` | direct standard-library verifier |
| Sections 2-4 and every lower bound | `lean/` | Lean 4 over Mathlib, kernel-checked; no `sorry`, no `native_decide`; see `lean/README.md` |

## Verification model

The computer-assisted statements follow the same pattern:

1. the paper gives a mathematical reduction to a finite collection of objects;
2. source code enumerates those objects or emits a complete SAT encoding;
3. frozen outputs are authenticated by SHA-256; and
4. a separate checker verifies coverage and terminal results.

For Proposition 6.1, the decisive proof objects are DRAT certificates checked
without trusting CaDiCaL.  For the intersecting bound 27, the decisive object
is an exhaustive-search ledger rather than a compact proof certificate.  The
public package therefore includes the reviewed source, regenerated frontier,
all 11,720 terminal records, total-node accounting, and small independent
controls.

The `f(3,4) <= 49` package uses complete rooted lists, profile enumeration,
and exhaustive cross-family ledgers.  Its structural inputs are reproducible
from source.  The four final ledgers are authenticated by SHA-256 and checked
for complete pair coverage, terminal results, and exact timeout/retry
correspondence.

## Verification

To check every artifact that is presently available:

```sh
./check_available.sh
```

This takes roughly two minutes on the publication machine.  It regenerates
the rooted-block and routing-cover inputs, checks all sixteen DRAT proofs,
audits the 105,917,089,577-node archived run, and verifies the 259-set
witness.

The Lean development is checked independently of the scripts above:
`cd lean && lake build` (requires the pinned toolchain via `elan`; details,
the statement-to-identifier table, and axiom-check instructions are in
`lean/README.md`).

For the complete release gate, including the four `f(3,4)` ledgers:

```sh
./check_all.sh
```

Required tools are Bash, Python 3, GCC or a compatible C compiler, GNU
`tar`, `zstd`, and `sha256sum`.  Regenerating Proposition 6.1 certificates
additionally requires PySAT 1.9.dev5 and CaDiCaL 3.0.0; checking the
published certificates does not.

## Verification certificates

`release-assets/prop_6_1_certificates.tar.zst` contains the SAT instances and
proof certificates for Proposition 6.1 (20 MB compressed, 348 MB expanded).
The verification scripts extract the archive and check all sixteen proofs
with the bundled checker, without rerunning the SAT solver.

## Abstract

Ultra-wideband (UWB) technology is known to have a high data rate in wireless communications due to its broad frequency range and low power consumption. Its flexibility enables a wide range of applications, including multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems, suited for advanced wireless communication systems. In this manuscript a novel meandered MIMO antenna, designed explicitly for UWB applications, is proposed and studied. The antenna features meandered strips arranged in a circular pattern, resembling a sunflower. The antenna structure is built on an FR4 with 24 × 24 × 1.6 mm^{3} size for a single element and 48 × 48 × 1.6 mm^{3} for the MIMO configuration. The antenna operates over a wide frequency range between 2.9 and 20 GHz, achieving a fractional bandwidth of 151%. In the MIMO configuration, it maintains good isolation, exceeding 15 dB across the entire operating band. The measured efficiency of the antenna surpasses 75%, with a peak gain of 5.9 dBi. Additionally, key parameters for MIMO performance include an envelope correlation coefficient (ECC) below 0.002, mean effective gain (MEG) less than −3 dB, channel capacity loss (CCL) under 0.25 bps/Hz, and a total active reflection coefficient (TARC) below −20 dB.

### 2.2. MIMO Configuration

After single element’s evolution and detailed analysis, four-element MIMO configuration is introduced. The elements are assigned in front by front and side-by-side manner. Figures 4(a) and 4(b) show the proposed MIMO antenna front and back side, respectively. As can be seen, the proposed MIMO system has a connected ground plane. The side-by-side elements have joint ground and a vertical strip connects the top-facing ground with a ring-shaped element at the middle. This also acts as a decoupling structure, enabling the antenna to have low mutual coupling. For better signal quality in UWB MIMO antenna, synergistic equalization techniques can be applied [6].

## What was actually shown

The manuscript claims a computer-assisted exclusion of 69-member three-sunflower-free four-uniform families, giving 54 <= M(4,3) <= 68. It improves the upper bound 83 in Axante et al., arXiv:2609.06175v1, Theorem 6.9. The classical lower construction is reproduced, not claimed as new. The proof combines their intersecting-family bound 27, structural point-link reductions, Jin's graph-homomorphism theorem, exact certificates and finite exhaustive checks. A local cap of 61 requires a complete R16 point-link and is not a global bound. Cardinality 68 is not excluded, the exact value is not determined, and the general sunflower conjecture (Erdős #20) remains open.

## What the AI did

The author reports using OpenAI Sol 5.6, Astra 6, Pro 6 and Sol 6.1. As disclosed in the manuscript, generative AI tools assisted proof development, software preparation and manuscript review. The named human author retains responsibility for the claims. The model names are the author's disclosure for this submission; the manuscript does not identify versions or attribute individual lemmas to particular models. Author-side AI reviews are not independent specialist verification.

## Verification

No independent mathematician has checked this yet. Checked by this site on 15 October 2026: the aiXiv v1 record and PDF open (CC BY, content-hashed, not withdrawn), the pinned GitHub commit 90c03c7 exists, and the manuscript's AI disclosure and Theorem 1.1 were read. Axante et al., arXiv:2609.06175v1 (still the only version), was read for Table 1, Proposition 6.7 (the imported bound 27) and Theorem 6.9 (54 <= f(4,3) <= 83). A separate script written here confirmed that the 54-member construction has no sunflower among its 24,804 triples, that no further four-set on its 18 points can be added, and that a graph with no three-edge sunflower has at most six edges (Lemma 3.1, on seven vertices). The companion's 42 finite suites (about 53 minutes) were not re-run here, nor was the imported exhaustive computation behind the bound 27, itself an AI-assisted preprint result from September 2026. The upper bound 68 rests on those computations and the written reductions; the author-side AI reviews are not independent.

# Transversal Six, Finite Obstructions and Boundary Profiles in Rank-Four Sunflower-Free Families

Version 13 · Final local edition · Evidence cutoff: 22 September 2026, America/New_York

Scope and review. This report distinguishes checked structural results, conditional implications and unresolved mathematical inputs. The accompanying immutable record documents the SuperMath X2 proof checks and SuperResearch X2.2 specialist rounds and governs local publication acceptance. Independent human certification is separate and is not claimed.

## Abstract

We continue a Lean development for finite families of distinct four-element sets containing no sunflower with three distinct members, including sunflowers with empty core. Two retained version-twelve structural advances concern the actual original family. First, if every closed meeting neighborhood has at least fifty-four members, degree seventeen is impossible; every supported point consequently has degree at least eighteen. The proof combines an exact local trace inequality with the separated eight/nine decomposition of a degree-seventeen link, forcing the impossible incidence equation 5k=9. 
The inherited local formalization establishes unconditional ceilings G(93) and I(41), lower-bound witnesses with fifty-four unrestricted members and twenty-seven intersecting members, and the conditional implication I(27)⇒G(81). An explicit witness of size twenty-seven supports a lower bound; it does not prove that all intersecting families have size at most twenty-seven. Throughout this report, I(27) remains an ordinary theorem parameter, rather than a project axiom or a result inferred from a paper's abstract.

Version eleven reduced a hypothetical eighty-one-member family, assuming I(27), to ten necessary degree profiles on seventeen or eighteen supported points. It also decomposed every degree-seventeen link in the large-meeting-neighborhood regime into intersecting components with eight and nine members and disjoint supports. The retained version-twelve argument uses that decomposition to exclude degree seventeen altogether. Eight of the ten version-eleven profiles consequently disappear, leaving two concrete possibilities on seventeen points.

## Results

### 1. A score of twenty-five forces a high companion

Proposition T1 (distinct companion). Suppose R∈F, |M(R)|≥54 and x∈R. If d(x)+$s_R(x)$≤25, then there exists y∈R with y≠x and d(y)=20. The strengthened public conclusion is checked in `Erdos20V12Profile.meeting_fifty_four_low_score_distinct_high_companion`, in the version-thirteen trace module.

Restrict first to M(R). Every degree at a point of R is unchanged because every member containing that point already meets R. The singleton trace at x is unchanged for the same reason. Label the four degrees a,b,c,d and the singleton counts $s_a$,$s_b$,$s_c$,$s_d$. Let $t_a$ be the number of exact traces on the three points of R other than the first, and define the other t-values similarly. Each t-value is zero or one. Set T=$t_a$+$t_b$+$t_c$+$t_d$.

Let S be the total singleton trace count and P the total pair trace count. The full trace is exactly the anchor itself. Thus |M(R)|=S+P+T+1 and the sum D of its four point degrees is S+2P+3T+4. If T=2, each companion score plus its own t-value is at most twenty-nine. Since $t_a$≤1, subtracting the other t-values bounds the total score by 111. If T≥3, the elementary bound on every companion score is twenty-nine, so the total is at most 112. Each case contradicts the displayed lower bound. At least one companion therefore has degree twenty.

The numerical argument does not by itself identify a member of F. The family-level bridge enumerates the sixteen possible intersections with R, supplies the exact full-trace count one, the pair- and triple-trace bounds, and the unchanged degrees after meeting restriction. It then restores the unordered anchor. This bridge prevents an arithmetic score condition from being used outside the setting in which it was derived. It also preserves y≠x when the ordered anchor is restored.

The threshold 25 is sharp for this numerical relaxation, without asserting sharpness for actual families. Singleton counts (8,9,9,9), six pair counts all 3, four triple counts all 0, and full trace 1 give meeting count 54, degrees (18,19,19,19), and distinguished score 26. All displayed weighted inequalities hold with no degree twenty. The closed Lean check `score_twenty_six_relaxation` verifies these numbers. The sixteen binary triple-trace cases are retained as an exact-integer diagnostic; for each case the upper bound under the absence of a high companion is strictly below 110+T. The cases do not purport to realize inconsistent premises.

### 2. Degree seventeen is impossible in the all-meeting54 regime

Theorem T2. If every closed meeting neighborhood of F has at least fifty-four members, no point has degree seventeen. Every supported point consequently has degree at least eighteen.

Assume d(x)=17. The inherited decomposition writes the actual triple link as $L_x$=A∪B, with |A|=8, |B|=9, both components intersecting and their supports disjoint. For completeness, the decomposition arises from the link's disjointness graph. The inherited score lower bound d(x)+$s_R(x)$≥25 makes its minimum degree at least eight. This graph is triangle-free, since three pairwise disjoint triples would be a sunflower. Because 5·8>2·17, the Andrásfai–Erdős–Sós theorem makes it bipartite [11], [12].

The color classes are intersecting triple families and have at most ten members each. Minimum degree eight and total size seventeen force class sizes eight and nine. Every vertex of the nine-class has eight neighbors, all in the eight-class; hence it is disjoint from every block of that class. This proves disjointness of supports, a stronger statement than disjointness of the two families as vertex sets.

For any P∈B, its disjoint neighbors in $L_x$ are exactly A. In the original member R={x}∪P, the singleton trace at x therefore has size eight. Its score is seventeen plus eight, equal to twenty-five. Proposition T1 forces a high point into R. This point is not x and hence lies in P. The inherited all-meeting54 high-independence theorem permits at most one high point in any member, so P contains exactly one.

Let K=supp(B)∩H. Every y∈K has original pair codegree d(x,y)=5: in the extremal link at the high center y, a supported point x occurs five times. The occurrence is positive because y lies in the support of B. Disjointness of the two component supports means that all link occurrences of y belong to B. Thus each y∈K occurs in exactly five blocks of B, whereas each block of B contains exactly one member of K. Counting incidences in the two orders gives

$$5|K|=\sum_{y\in K}|\{P\in B:y\in P\}|=\sum_{P\in B}|P\cap K|=9.$$

This is impossible over the natural numbers. The supported-degree lower bound eighteen follows from the inherited lower bound seventeen. The proof does not require either component to extend to a ten-design, nor does it assert a six-point support for the nine-component. It uses only the actual separated decomposition, the high-center codegree and the exact trace bridge.

# Lean formalisation

Lean 4 formalisation of the combinatorial results of the paper
*Sunflower-Free Uniform Families: Recursive Constructions and Explicit
Bounds*.  The development covers the main combinatorial arguments of
Sections 2–4, the appendix capacity recurrence, and every explicit finite
witness used for the numerical lower bounds.

## Toolchain

- Lean: `leanprover/lean4:v4.33.1` (pinned in `lean-toolchain`)
- Mathlib: tag `v4.33.1` (pinned in `lakefile.toml`)

Build with `lake build` from this directory. The development contains no
`sorry`, uses no `native_decide`, and every theorem below is certified by
Lean's kernel to depend only on the three standard axioms
(`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`); check any theorem with
`#print axioms Sunflower.<name>`.

## Reading the proofs

The public definitions and theorem statements are the best starting point for
checking the mathematics.  Some recurring Lean proof syntax translates as
follows:

- `obtain ⟨x, hx⟩ := h` unpacks an existential proof `h : ∃ x, P x` into a
  witness `x` and a proof `hx : P x`.  With conjunctions it similarly names
  the component proofs.  It does not add an assumption or invoke automation.
- `rcases h with ...` is the same kind of pattern unpacking, with support for
  alternatives such as `h₁ | h₂`.
- `refine ⟨..., ?_, ...⟩` supplies the displayed parts of a constructor and
  leaves each `?_` as an explicit remaining goal.
- `simpa [defs] using h` simplifies both the type of `h` and the current goal,
  then checks that they coincide.  `rwa [eqs] at h` rewrites `h` and closes the
  goal with the rewritten result.
- `tac₁ <;> tac₂` runs `tac₂` on every goal produced by `tac₁`.
- `omega` proves the remaining Presburger-arithmetic goal; the relevant
  inequalities are normally named immediately before it in the main proofs.

Tagged construction inputs have named views `TaggedFWitData` and
`TaggedPsiWitData`.  Thus `A.isUniform`, `A.sunflowerFree`, `A.matchingLT`,
`A.card_eq`, and `A.taggedBy` state the role of each fact directly.  Small
two- or three-component `obtain` expressions are retained where they simply
unpack a local membership or existence statement.

## Encoding

The finiteness of `f(w,k)` rests on the Erdős–Rado theorem, which Mathlib
does not have, so `f` and `ψ` are not defined as numbers. Each quantity is a
pair of predicates on sizes:

- `FBound w k n` / `FWit w k n` — every family has at most `n` members /
  some family has exactly `n` members (`f(w,k) = n` is the conjunction);
- `PsiBound w k m n` / `PsiWit w k m n` — the same with the matching cap

# Lean formalisation

Lean 4 formalisation of the combinatorial results of the paper
*Sunflower-Free Uniform Families: Recursive Constructions and Explicit
Bounds*.  The development covers the main combinatorial arguments of
Sections 2–4, the appendix capacity recurrence, and every explicit finite
witness used for the numerical lower bounds.

## Toolchain

- Lean: `leanprover/lean4:v4.33.1` (pinned in `lean-toolchain`)
- Mathlib: tag `v4.33.1` (pinned in `lakefile.toml`)

Build with `lake build` from this directory. The development contains no
`sorry`, uses no `native_decide`, and every theorem below is certified by
Lean's kernel to depend only on the three standard axioms
(`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`); check any theorem with
`#print axioms Sunflower.<name>`.

## Reading the proofs

The public definitions and theorem statements are the best starting point for
checking the mathematics.  Some recurring Lean proof syntax translates as
follows:

- `obtain ⟨x, hx⟩ := h` unpacks an existential proof `h : ∃ x, P x` into a
  witness `x` and a proof `hx : P x`.  With conjunctions it similarly names
  the component proofs.  It does not add an assumption or invoke automation.
- `rcases h with ...` is the same kind of pattern unpacking, with support for
  alternatives such as `h₁ | h₂`.
- `refine ⟨..., ?_, ...⟩` supplies the displayed parts of a constructor and
  leaves each `?_` as an explicit remaining goal.
- `simpa [defs] using h` simplifies both the type of `h` and the current goal,
  then checks that they coincide.  `rwa [eqs] at h` rewrites `h` and closes the
  goal with the rewritten result.
- `tac₁ <;> tac₂` runs `tac₂` on every goal produced by `tac₁`.
- `omega` proves the remaining Presburger-arithmetic goal; the relevant
  inequalities are normally named immediately before it in the main proofs.

Tagged construction inputs have named views `TaggedFWitData` and
`TaggedPsiWitData`.  Thus `A.isUniform`, `A.sunflowerFree`, `A.matchingLT`,
`A.card_eq`, and `A.taggedBy` state the role of each fact directly.  Small
two- or three-component `obtain` expressions are retained where they simply
unpack a local membership or existence statement.

The finiteness of `f(w,k)` rests on the Erdős–Rado theorem, which Mathlib

  subtraction).

aiXiv:2610.02233 [pdf] digest pick Claude AI-derived

Landau-Siegel zeros over a base field and effective Brauer-Siegel

William D. Banks

Comments: 19 pages, 6 diagrams

Subjects: Number Theory (math.NT)

Real zeros of quadratic L-functions over a fixed number field admit an effective repulsion bound, which upgrades the Brauer–Siegel theorem to an effective and uniform statement over all Galois extensions of that base — the case Stark had to omit because quadratic subfields carried Siegel's ineffectivity. The mechanism is a uniform bound on Chebotarev sums in which the field enters only through a computable lattice invariant, a tool of independent use for effective class-number and L-function estimates.

An explicit elementary proof of no Landau--Siegel zeros

Victor Zhenyu Guo

Comments: Comments are welcome

Subjects: Number Theory (math.NT)

For every primitive quadratic character of conductor q ≥ 3, each real zero of its Dirichlet L-function is claimed to satisfy (1−β)log q > 1/100, with all constants explicit and no separate treatment of small conductors. If correct this removes the exceptional-zero obstruction from analytic number theory, making Siegel's theorem and class number bounds effective.

aiXiv:2610.02124 [pdf] digest pick ChatGPT 6.0 AI-assisted

Ramified convolution and monodromy bases for symmetrizable Kac--Moody algebras

Jiarui Fei

Comments: Symmetrizable Cartan matrix, preprojective species, convolution algebra, monodromy, semicanonical basis, crystal

Subjects: Representation Theory (math.RT); Rings and Algebras (math.RA)

Convolution on a ramified preprojective species over C((t)), with structure constants given by alternating traces of tame monodromy, realizes the positive enveloping algebra of any symmetrizable Kac-Moody algebra and yields an integral basis that specializes to Lusztig's semicanonical basis when the Cartan matrix is symmetric. The construction proves the Geiss-Leclerc-Schroer acyclic convolution conjecture for all symmetrizable Cartan matrices and all positive integral symmetrizers, and produces a counterexample to their Support Conjecture.

aiXiv:2610.02123 [pdf] digest pick OpenAI ChatGPT AI-assisted

A smoothly bounded pseudoconvex domain with incomplete Kobayashi distance

Armen Edigarian

Subjects: Complex Variables (math.CV)

There is a bounded pseudoconvex domain in C^3 with smooth boundary and smooth plurisubharmonic defining function whose Kobayashi and Caratheodory distances are incomplete, so boundary smoothness does not imply Kobayashi completeness. Finite D'Angelo type does imply it, with explicit lower bounds on the Kobayashi–Royden metric, and in particular every bounded pseudoconvex domain with real-analytic boundary is Kobayashi complete.

# How agent traces work

A trace is the record of a session in which an AI system took part in the work: the exchanges, the system's reasoning, the tool calls and their output, the attempts that failed. On aiXiv it sits next to the paper, under the author's name, with the date recorded and a SHA-256 hash of the file. Readers open it as a transcript; the file itself stays as uploaded.

Traces are attached by the paper's owner from the paper's attach page (`https://aixiv.online/attach/<id>`, reached after claiming or submitting). There are four ways, and the first is usually the whole job.

## 1 · The agent uploads its own sessions

The attach page shows a short prompt with a paper-scoped token. Pasted into the agent that did the work, in the project where it happened, the agent reads attach.md, finds its own session files on disk, runs a dry run that reports what will be redacted, uploads the raw files, and reports the hashes. It is told not to write a summary, and the page shows what arrived.
API keys and tokens, and the user name inside absolute paths, are redacted by default; email addresses and IP addresses on request. Counts are shown on the paper page (“2 keys, 87 paths redacted”), never hidden. Archives and PDFs are stored as-is. Owners can remove a trace at any time; removal deletes the file.

Readers see each trace listed under “AI process” on the paper page with agent, model, dates, turn count, hash, and the owner's one-line note, and can open the transcript or download the file.

## The aixiv command line

`npx aixiv@latest login`approve once in the browser; the token is stored locally

`npx aixiv@latest publish`publish the paper in this folder, dry run first

`npx aixiv@latest sessions`list this project's sessions across hosts

`npx aixiv@latest attach --token TOKEN --session current`this session, from inside Claude Code or Codex

`npx aixiv@latest attach --token TOKEN --agent codex --session latest --role proof`the latest Codex session of this project, labelled

`npx aixiv@latest attach --token TOKEN --agent cursor`pick Cursor chats to export and upload
If the host does not write sessions to disk at all, there is nothing to upload from it; use the chat app's export or share link instead.

Which sessions should be attached?

The ones that mattered: where the idea appeared, where the proof was found, where it was checked, and the ones that failed in an informative way. A full set with a note is welcome too. Label each with a role (discovery, proof, verification, formalization, writing, failed exploration) and, if useful, what it points to (“Lemma 3.2”).

The file is huge.

Session files with long tool output reach hundreds of megabytes. The limit is 250 MB per request; zip larger sets or upload in parts. Transcripts over 64 MB are stored and downloadable but not rendered in the page.

Something private is in the transcript.

Keys and user paths are redacted on upload. For anything else, redact the file locally first, or remove the trace and re-upload. Removal deletes the stored file.

Can traces be attached now and shown later?

Today a trace is public as soon as it is attached. If you need an embargo (attach now, show after acceptance), write to [email protected]; it is on the list.

Under what license?

Traces are shown under the paper's listing terms unless the owner states otherwise in the note. A per-trace license choice is planned.

The token stopped working.

Attach tokens expire after 180 days and are tied to the owner; the attach page always shows the current one and can reset it. Account tokens from Settings also work with every attach command.

Windows paths and user names.

Claude Code on Windows keeps sessions under `%USERPROFILE%\.claude\projects\`; the CLI resolves this. Path redaction covers `C:\Users\<name>` as well as `/Users` and `/home`.

Can a research agent attach traces without a human at the keyboard?

Yes: the REST endpoint and the MCP tool accept the token directly, so a harness can attach its own sessions at the end of a run. See attach.md and skill.md.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

> Abstract: We consider the DMPK ensemble, which models quantum transport in a disordered wire, and describe its limiting local statistics as the number of particles tends to infinity. In the metallic regime, as well as at crossover I, we obtain sine statistics in the bulk, Bessel statistics at the hard edge and Airy statistics at the soft edge. In the insulating regime, we prove localization around certain explicit deterministic positions with Gaussian fluctuations. This confirms and quantifies the predicted universal and localized behavior in the physics literature. At crossover II, we obtain explicit limiting kernels in the bulk and at both edges, which interpolate between these regimes. The hard edge kernel involves Legendre functions and, to the best of our knowledge, is new, while the bulk and soft edge kernels agree with those derived for the squared singular values of critically scaled products of independent Ginibre matrices. Summary:  | The DMPK ensemble's local statistics are identified in every regime: sine, Bessel and Airy kernels in the metallic phase, localization with Gaussian fluctuations in the insulating phase, and new interpolating kernels including a hard-edge kernel built from Legendre functions, with the conductance variance converging to 1/15 across the metallic regime. A class of invariant pseudo-unitary matrices closed under multiplication realizes the ensemble as the spectral law of a random matrix product, accounting for its agreement with critically scaled Ginibre products.

# Sunflower

A sunflower, also called a delta-system, is a family of at least two distinct sets whose pairwise intersections are all equal. For members Image: A_1, Image: A_2, ..., Image: A_r, there is a set Image: C such that

Image: A_i intersection A_j=C   | (1)

whenever Image: i!=j. The set Image: C is the core or kernel, and the sets Image: A_i\C are the petals. The petals are pairwise disjoint. The core may be empty, so a family of pairwise disjoint sets is a sunflower. For example, Image: {1,2}, Image: {1,3}, and Image: {1,4} form a three-member sunflower with core Image: {1}.

A sunflower in this combinatorial sense is distinct from the flower-like figures called daisies and the Vogel spiral models of phyllotaxis.

## What was actually shown

The manuscript claims a computer-assisted exclusion of 69-member three-sunflower-free four-uniform families, giving 54 <= M(4,3) <= 68. It improves the upper bound 83 in Axante et al., arXiv:2609.06175v1, Theorem 6.9. The classical lower construction is reproduced, not claimed as new. The proof combines their intersecting-family bound 27, structural point-link reductions, Jin's graph-homomorphism theorem, exact certificates and finite exhaustive checks. A local cap of 61 requires a complete R16 point-link and is not a global bound. Cardinality 68 is not excluded, the exact value is not determined, and the general sunflower conjecture (Erdős #20) remains open.

### Exact statement

For every fixed integer r >= 3, prove or disprove that there is a constant C_r such that every family of more than C_r^k sets of size at most k contains an r-petal sunflower.

### Why it matters

A proof would give a purely exponential threshold forcing a sunflower: sets sharing one common core and otherwise disjoint. It would quantify when sufficiently large set families must contain this reusable combinatorial pattern.

# Frankl-complete sunflowers and extremal families of four-sets

LM Liu Mingchang

View Full Paper

## Key Points

  * Characterize Frankl-complete sunflowers of four-sets and resolve the four-uniform case of Morris's asymptotic conjecture regarding extremal union-closed families.
  * Formulated a charging inequality distributing weight three to the core and weight one to petals across admissible families.
  * Combined elementary extremal estimates with computer-assisted exhaustive search algorithms and explicit certificate constructions.
  * Proved that a sunflower with a two-point core and disjoint two-point petals is Frankl-complete if and only if it contains at least nine petals.
  * Resolved the four-uniform case of Morris's conjecture by showing FC(4,n) = Θ(n²).
  * Established FC(4,9) = 16 using a fifteen-block negative certificate and refuted a lexicographic extremality conjecture of Pulaj and Wood.

## Implication

Mathematical analysis demonstrates Frankl-completeness for nine-petal sunflowers in four-uniform families, resolving the four-uniform case of Morris's asymptotic conjecture.

### Abstract

A finite configuration is Frankl-complete if every union-closed extension has an element of the original support in at least half of its members. We prove that a sunflower consisting of a two-point core and disjoint two-point petals is Frankl-complete if and only if it has at least nine petals. The positive direction follows from a charging inequality valid for every admissible family, with weight three on the core and weight one on the petals. Combining this criterion with an elementary extremal estimate gives FC(4,n) = Θ(n²), resolving the four-uniform case of Morris’s asymptotic conjecture. Independently, we establish FC(4,9) = 16 by an explicit fifteen-block negative certificate and a computer-assisted exhaustive upper bound. A smaller positive certificate also refutes a lexicographic extremality conjecture of Pulaj and Wood. We give further finite bounds and explain why higher-uniformity sunflowers cannot provide the same local forcing mechanism. Version V1. Code and exact certificates are available in the companion repository: https://github.com/michaeliu4/frankl-complete-four-sets/releases/tag/V1

## What was actually shown

The manuscript claims a computer-assisted exclusion of 69-member three-sunflower-free four-uniform families, giving 54 <= M(4,3) <= 68. It improves the upper bound 83 in Axante et al., arXiv:2609.06175v1, Theorem 6.9. The classical lower construction is reproduced, not claimed as new. A local cap of 61 requires a complete R16 point-link and is not a global bound. \begin{abstract}
Let $ M(4,3)$ be the maximum size of a finite simple family of four-element
sets containing no three distinct members whose pairwise intersections are
equal. The empty intersection is included in the forbidden configurations.
We give a computer-assisted exclusion of families of size $69$,
giving the bound $54\le M(4,3)\le 68$. The argument combines an
imported bound of $27$ for intersecting families, structural analysis of
point-links, exact trace constraints and finite exhaustions. The proof is
organized at the cardinality $69$. A cap on families containing a complete $ R16$ point-link
provides a shorter final contradiction. We make the imported results,
computational lemma contracts and remaining verification limits explicit.
The lower construction is classical. Neither exclusion of size $68$ nor
optimality of the lower construction is claimed.
\end{abstract}
\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} Sunflowers; four-uniform families; extremal set theory;
exact certificates.



\section{The finite extremal problem}
\label{sec:introduction}
A three-sunflower is a triple of distinct sets $ A,B,C $ such that
\[
 A\cap B=A\cap C=B\cap C.
\]
The common intersection is the kernel. Allowing the empty kernel means that
three pairwise disjoint sets are also forbidden. Throughout, families are
simple: a set occurs at most once.

The quantity studied here is
\[
 M(4,3)=\max\{\lvert\F\rvert:\F\text{ is a finite simple
 four-uniform family without a three-sunflower}\}.
\]
Thus an upper bound $68$ is equivalent to saying that every such family of
\emph{at least $69$} sets contains a three-sunflower. The convention that
counts the first cardinality forcing a sunflower adds one to $ M $.

\begin{theorem}[Computer-assisted bound]
\label{thm:main}
With H27 and the classification and finite-exclusion lemmas stated in this
manuscript, no simple four-uniform three-sunflower-free family of size $69$
exists. Consequently,
\[
 \boxed{54\le M(4,3)\le 68}.
\]
\end{theorem}

The general sunflower conjecture of Erd\H{o}s and Rado~\cite{ER1960}
concerns exponential dependence on the
uniformity for each fixed number of petals. A bound for this particular
four-uniform case does not resolve that asymptotic conjecture. The distinction
also prevents a finite improvement from being described as a solution of the
entire Erd\H{o}s problem.

The contemporary primary comparison is the preprint of Axante et al.
\cite{AXB2026}, whose Theorem~6.9 gives $54\le f(4,3)\le83$, with $ f $
defined there as the maximum sunflower-free size. Their Proposition~6.7
proves that an intersecting four-uniform three-sunflower-free family has at
most $27$ members, and Proposition~6.8 gives equality. We use the upper bound
as an imported theorem, denoted H27. It is not a claim that general
three-uniform families have maximum $27$.

The lower bound $54$ is attributed to Abbott and Hanson
\cite{AH1974} in the table of Axante et al. We reproduce the construction
and its elementary verification in Section~\ref{sec:lower}. No new lower
bound or priority for that construction is asserted. The numerical
comparison with $83$ provides the comparison for this bound; it does not by
itself establish that $68$ is a new record. The historical upper
bound $142$ of Abbott, Hanson and Sauer~\cite{AHS1972} is also
reported in that table; the numerical attribution here is through
the checked preprint rather than a new reading of the original article.



The imported intersecting-family theorem and the exact finite lemmas are
stated with their domains. The companion provides the complete named
finite verification route; the written reductions establish why these
finite domains cover every hypothetical family.

\section{Notation and the proof architecture}
\label{sec:notation}
We abbreviate a finite simple $r$-uniform three-sunflower-free family
as SF$r$; the forbidden configurations include the empty kernel.
Only points that occur in a member of $\F $ belong to its support. Write
$ d(x)=\lvert\{A\in\F:x\in A\}\rvert $ and
$ d(x,y)=\lvert\{A\in\F:\{x,y\}\subseteq A\}\rvert $. For $ R\in\F $,
\[
 N_{\F}[R]=\{A\in\F:A\cap R\ne\varnothing\},\qquad
 D_{\F}(R)=\{A\in\F:A\cap R=\varnothing\},
\]
and $\mu(\F)=\min_{R\in\F}\lvert N_{\F}[R]\rvert $.
The neighborhood is closed: it includes $ R $ itself. The point-link
\[
 L_x=\{A\setminus\{x\}:A\in\F,\ x\in A\}
\]
is a complete link of the ambient family. A point degree in $ L_x $ is the
global codegree $ d(x,y)$, not the global degree $ d(y)$.

\begin{lemma}[The neighborhood lower bound]
\label{lem:h27}
If $\F $ is three-sunflower-free, then $ D_{\F}(R)$ is intersecting for every
$ R\in\F $. Under H27,
\[
 \lvert N_{\F}[R]\rvert\ge\lvert\F\rvert-27.
\]
In particular, a hypothetical family of size $69$ has $\mu\ge 42$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If two members of $ D_{\F}(R)$ were disjoint, they and $ R $ would be a
sunflower with empty kernel. H27 applies to this intersecting subfamily,
which is still four-uniform, simple and sunflower-free.
\end{proof}

The disjointness graph has the \emph{members} of $\F $ as vertices; two are
adjacent exactly when they are disjoint. This graph is triangle-free.
Its degree at $ R $ is $\lvert\F\rvert-\lvert N_{\F}[R]\rvert $.
Homomorphism fibers in this graph consist of members of $\F $, whereas the
degrees and codegrees above count points. Maintaining this distinction is
essential to the incidence arguments.

Our imported graph theorem is due to Jin~\cite{JIN1993}, in the exact
form stated as Theorem~A by Nikiforov~\cite{NIK2010}: for
$1\le k\le 9$, every triangle-free graph of order $n$ with
minimum degree strictly greater than $(k+1)n/(3k+2)$ is homomorphic
to the Andr\'asfai graph $A_k$. Its cyclic definition is given in
Section~\ref{sec:fibrebridge}. We verify the strict inequality at
$k=3$ or $k=4$ in each use; equality does not suffice.

The proof follows three reductions. First, universal link bounds and
cardinality-$69$ trace constraints exclude maximum point degrees
$20,19,18,17$ and at most $15$. In the remaining maximum-$16$ case, a
triangle-free graph homomorphism and a near-transversal argument force
every degree-$16$ point to have a complete $ R16$ link. Finally, the
local $ R61$ lemma contradicts $\lvert\F\rvert=69$. The first
reduction and all finite coverings are recorded with their hypotheses;
none is transferred from cardinality $70$ without its own bridge.

\section{Elementary link structure}
\label{sec:foundations}
\subsection{Graphs without three-sunflowers}
\begin{lemma}
\label{lem:sf2}
A simple graph contains no three-sunflower of edges if and only if its
maximum degree and matching number are both at most two. It has at most
six edges. Equality gives two vertex-disjoint triangles.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The two possible kernels of a three-sunflower of distinct edges are a
single vertex and the empty set. They respectively give a three-edge
star and a three-edge matching. Every nontrivial component of a graph
with maximum degree two is a path or a cycle. With matching number $ q $,
a path has at most $2q $ edges; an even cycle has $2q $ and an odd cycle
$2q+1$. The total matching number is at most two, so the maximum six
edges is attained precisely by two triangles. With five edges the
possibilities are a five-cycle or a triangle and a two-edge path.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The canonical ten- and eight-member families}
\label{sec:canonical}
We abbreviate $\{0,1,2\}$ as $012$ when all labels are single digits. Put
\[
 \Pten=\{012,015,023,034,045,124,134,135,235,245\}.
\]
This intersecting family has ten triples, every point degree five and
every pair codegree two. Every point-link is a five-cycle, so it is
three-sunflower-free. Write $ P_9$ and $ P_8$ for subfamilies obtained by
deleting respectively one and two blocks of $\Pten $.

On seven distinct points let
\[
 Q(h,k;T;a,b)=\{\{h\}\cup S,\{k\}\cup S:S\in\binom{T}{2}\}
 \cup\{\{h,k,a\},\{h,k,b\}\},\qquad |T|=3.
\]
This is the eight-member family $ Q_8$. The points $ h,k $ are its hubs,
$ T $ its triad and $ a,b $ its leaves. The hubs have degree five, the triad
points degree four and the leaves degree one. Pair codegrees are at
most two, and every point-link has matching number at most two.

\begin{proposition}[Intersecting triple classification]
\label{prop:i810}
An intersecting three-uniform three-sunflower-free family has at most
ten members. At ten it is $\Pten $; at nine it is $ P_9$; at eight it is
$ P_8$ or $ Q_8$, up to relabeling.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Every point-link is a graph from Lemma~\ref{lem:sf2}, so its point
degrees are at most six. A degree-six point has two triangles as its
link. A triple avoiding it would have to cover both triangles with
only three points, which is impossible; the whole family then has
only six members. A degree-five point has link either a five-cycle
or a triangle and a two-edge path. In the first case every triple
avoiding the point is one of the five three-point vertex covers of
the cycle, giving a subfamily of $\Pten $. In the second case there
are at most three such triples, and at size eight all three occur,
giving $ Q_8$.

We justify the existence of a degree-five point at sizes at least
eight. For an intersecting family $\mathcal H $ of $ m $ triples,
every $ A\in\mathcal H $ satisfies
\[
 \sum_{x\in A}d_{\mathcal H}(x)\ge m+2.
\]
If all degrees are at most four this gives $ m\le 10$; at $ m=10$ all
used points would have degree four, contrary to a degree sum of $30$.
At $ m=9$ all used points have degree three or four. If their number
is $ n $, and $ B $ counts pairs of points of codegree two, counting
intersections of pairs of triples gives $ B=45-6n $. The degree sum
$27$ and $ B\ge 0$ force $ n=7,B=3$. The triples would use
$27-B=24$ distinct pairs on seven points, exceeding $\binom 72=21$.

At $ m=8$ and maximum degree four all used degrees are at least two.
Let $ a,b,c $ count degrees two, three, four. Then $ a+b+c=n $ and
$2a+3b+4c=24$. Intersection counting gives $ B=20-3n+c $.
For each point the number $ r(x)$ of codegree-two neighbors is at
least $ d(x)-2$: the line graph of its point-link has independence
number at most two, whereas deleting at most one endpoint per edge
gives an independent set of size at least $ d(x)-r(x)$. Consequently
$2B\ge b+2c $, so $40-6n\ge b $ and $ n\le 6$. The degree sum forces
$ n=6$ and all degrees four. Now $ B=8$, so the eight triples use
$24-B=16$ distinct pairs on six points, exceeding $15$. This final
contradiction completes the classification without a support cutoff.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Isolation and a separated neighborhood}
\begin{lemma}[Isolation]
\label{lem:isolation}
In a sunflower-free triple family containing $ P_{10},P_9$ or $ P_8$,
every additional triple meeting the six-point support is one of the
deleted blocks. For $ Q(h,k;T;a,b)$, every additional triple meeting
the five-point core $\{h,k\}\cup T $ is $\{h,a,b\}$ or $\{k,a,b\}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $ P_{10}$ all pairs on its support already have codegree two.
Meeting the support in one point gives a third disjoint edge in
that point-link, using a matching of size two in a five-cycle.
For $ P_9$ or $ P_8$, a new internal triple can use only pairs of the
deleted blocks. The only triangles in the union of those one or
two triangles are the deleted blocks themselves. A single-point
intersection is still excluded by a matching of size two in a
five-cycle with at most two edges removed. For a two-point
intersection $ ij $, choose an endpoint contained in just one deleted
block if the pair has remaining codegree one. Its link is a
four-edge path with the other endpoint at an end; after removing
that endpoint a matching of size two remains. If the pair has
remaining codegree zero, the two deleted blocks both contain it;
removing their two incident edges again leaves a three-edge path
with matching number two. These matchings create a forbidden
singleton-kernel sunflower with the new triple.

All ten pairs of the $ Q_8$ core have codegree two. A new triple
cannot use two core points. A single triad point has a matching of
size two within the core, which excludes it. For a single hub,
its link consists of the triad triangle and the two edges joining
the other hub to the leaves. Unless both leaves occur in the new
triple, one of those two edges and an edge of the triangle avoid
its remaining points and form a forbidden matching. This leaves
only the two stated triples.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[B4 separation]
\label{lem:b4}
Let $ A $ belong to a sunflower-free triple family $\L $. If at least
eight members of $\L $ are disjoint from $ A $, its closed neighborhood
$ N_{\L}[A]$ is intersecting and has at most ten members.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The disjoint members form an intersecting family $\mathcal H $.
Proposition~\ref{prop:i810} classifies it. For a $ P $-type, isolation
forces every member of the remaining part to avoid its support:
deleted blocks cannot occur there, since they are also disjoint
from $ A $ and would belong to $\mathcal H $. Two disjoint remaining
members and a member of $\mathcal H $ would be an empty-kernel
sunflower. For $ Q_8$, the same argument uses the five-point core;
the two exceptional triples of Lemma~\ref{lem:isolation} are
disjoint from $ A $ and cannot belong to the remaining part. A
core-only block of $ Q_8$ gives the required empty-kernel sunflower
if two remaining members were disjoint. The intersecting bound
of ten now applies.
\end{proof}

The $ Q_8$ conclusion uses only core isolation. Its leaves may be
shared by the remaining part; treating all seven support points
as isolated would be incorrect.

\begin{corollary}
\label{cor:triple20}
The maximum size of a simple three-uniform family without a
three-sunflower is $20$. Therefore in a four-uniform such family,
\[
 d(x)\le 20,\qquad d(x,y)\le 6,\qquad d(x,y,z)\le 2.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Relative to a triple $ A $, an exact singleton class has at most
three members and an exact pair class at most one. The residues
are intersecting sunflower-free graphs or singleton families,
respectively. Thus $|N_{\L}[A]|\le 13$. If $|\L|\ge 21$, at least
eight members avoid $ A $; B4 bounds the neighborhood by ten, and
its disjoint intersecting part also has size at most ten, a
contradiction. Two copies of $\Pten $ on disjoint supports give
twenty members. The point, pair and triple links of a four-uniform
family now give the three displayed caps.
\end{proof}

\section{Exact traces and the near-transversal argument}
\label{sec:traces}
For $ R\in\F $, let $ s_x,p_{xy},t_m $ count members with exact trace
$\{x\},\{x,y\},R\setminus\{m\}$ on $ R $. Put
$ S=\sum s_x $, $ P=\sum p_{xy}$ and $ T=\sum t_m $. Then
\[
 |N_{\F}[R]|=1+S+P+T,\qquad
 \sum_{x\in R}d(x)=4+S+2P+3T.
\]
Exact residues are intersecting and sunflower-free: two disjoint
residues with $ R $ give a sunflower with their exact trace as
kernel. In particular $ s_x\le 10,p_{xy}\le 3,t_m\le 1$.
For $ r_x=\sum_{y\ne x}p_{xy}$, the part of $ L_x $ meeting
$ R\setminus\{x\}$ has size
\[
 k_x=1+r_x+T-t_x,\qquad d(x)=s_x+k_x.
\]
When $ s_x\ge 8$, B4 makes this part intersecting. The trace
constraints keep the actual external points shared by its members;
separate integer histograms do not certify their compatibility.

Call a four-point set a \emph{complete transversal} of a triple
family if it meets every member. Relative to $ A\in\L $, a
\emph{near-transversal} is a four-point set avoiding $ A $ and
meeting every other member of $\L $.

\begin{lemma}[A near-transversal is unique]
\label{lem:near}
Let $\L $ be an SF3 family with $16$ members and, for some
$ A_0\in\L $, a B4 separation $ H=D_{\L}(A_0)$,
$ K=N_{\L}[A_0]$ into two intersecting parts of size eight.
If it has a complete
four-point transversal, each $ A\in\L $ has at most one
near-transversal.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The parts are $ P_8$ or $ Q_8$. If a part is $ P_8$, its support
is isolated from the other part. If $ H $ is $ P_8$, its deleted blocks are disjoint from
$ A_0$ and cannot belong to $ K $. If $ K $ is $ P_8$ and one member
of $ H $ is a deleted block on its support, intersection of $ H $
forces all eight members of $ H $ to meet that support; isolation
would restrict them to at most two deleted blocks, a contradiction.
Meeting at least seven members
requires at least two points from its support, since its maximum
point degree is five. All four transversal points are therefore
allocated two to each part. For two $ Q_8$ parts, their five-point
cores are disjoint; only leaves may be shared. Indeed, isolation
forces $ K $ to avoid the core of $ H $: both exceptional triples avoid
$ A_0$ and would belong to $ H $. Conversely a member of $ H $ meeting
the core of $ K $ would have to be one of its two exceptional triples;
this is impossible since every member of $ H $ uses core points of
$ H $, which lie outside the entire support of $ K $.
Each core has six
core-only triples, and each point occurs in at most four of them.
Meeting at least five core-only triples in each part requires
two points in each core. Again all four points are allocated.

A $ P_8$ part with a two-point cover must have its two deleted
blocks intersecting in two points. The $60$ automorphisms of
$\Pten $ act transitively on these $15$ pairs of deleted blocks
(out of $45$). We may take
$ P^*=\Pten\setminus\{012,015\}$, whose unique complete
two-point cover is $34$. For the canonical $ Q_8$ with hubs
$0,1$, triad $2,3,4$ and leaves $5,6$, the unique cover is $01$.
The two-point near-transversals are exactly the following:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{cccc}
\toprule
$ P^*$ block & Near-cover & $ Q_8$ block & Near-cover\\
\midrule
$023$ & $45$ & $023$ & $14$\\
$034$ & none & $024$ & $13$\\
$045$ & $23$ & $034$ & $12$\\
$124$ & $35$ & $123$ & $04$\\
$134$ & none & $124$ & $03$\\
$135$ & $24$ & $134$ & $02$\\
$235$ & none & $015$ & none\\
$245$ & none & $016$ & none\\

\end{center}
For an omitted block in one part, the two points in the other
part form its unique complete cover; the first pair is unique
when it exists by the table. This proves the assertion with

\texttt{primary\_check.py}; the reduction above, rather than a

\end{proof}

\section{The universal sixteen-link classification}
\label{sec:r16classification}

For an SF3 family $ L $, write $ D_L(T)=\{U\in L:U\cap T=\varnothing\}$ and
$\rho(L)=\max_{T\in L}|D_L(T)|$. In this paper, ``R16'' means
$|L|=16$ and $\rho(L)\le 7$, together with the SF3 condition. It is not an
assertion that all SF3 families of size 16 are impossible.

\begin{theorem}[Universal R16 classification]\label{thm:r16class}
Every R16 is isomorphic to the following family. Take four distinct hubs
$ K=\{u,v,a,b\}$ and two disjoint three-element sets $ D,E $, disjoint also
from $ K $. Then
\[
 R=\{i\cup P:i\in\{u,v\},\ P\in\tbinom D2\}
 \cup\tbinom K3
 \cup\{i\cup Q:i\in\{a,b\},\ Q\in\tbinom E2\}.
\]
Here and below, a point in a union denotes its singleton. The proof uses
the explicitly certified finite computations described below.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
We first classify the possible seven-member intersecting family that will
occur as $ D_L(T)$. Its support has at most seven points. Here is an
arbitrary-support proof of this reduction. A degree-six point would force
only six triples: a triple avoiding it cannot cover two disjoint triangles.
For maximum degree at most four and no degree-one point, let $ b,c,d $ count
points of degrees 2,3,4. Then $2b+3c+4d=21$. If $ B $ counts used pairs of
codegree two, counting intersections gives $ B=b+3c+6d-21$.
For a point $ w $, its SF2 link has matching number at most two; if $ r(w)$
counts its codegree-two neighbours, $ r(w)\ge d(w)-2$. Hence
$2B\ge c+2d $, or $2d\ge 2b+c $. Together with
$21=3n-b+d $, this implies $ n\le 7$. Equality would force $ b=d,c=0$ and
$ n=2d $, impossible for $ n=7$. Thus this case has support at most six.

If $\ell uv $ contains a degree-one point $\ell $, the other six triples
meet $\{u,v\}$. Their distributions between only $ u $, only $ v $, and both
are $(3,3,0)$ or $(3,2,1)$, after interchanging $ u,v $. A three-edge
intersecting SF2 family is a triangle; cross-intersection confines the
two residual graphs to the same triad. The first case has support six;
the second has support seven. Finally, for a degree-five point, its
link is $ C_5$ or $ K_3\sqcup P_3$, where $ P_3$ has two edges. A triple
avoiding the point must be a three-vertex cover. In the cycle case it
lies on those five vertices; in the other case it contains two vertices
of the triangle and the middle vertex of the path. This gives support
six or the unique seven-point model, respectively.

The finite catalogue on six points is complete: every intersecting
seven-triple family selects seven of the ten complementary pairs of
triples, choosing one side from each. This gives
$\binom{10}{7}2^7=15360$ choices. The checker reconstructs all 1860 SF3

\begin{lemma}[Maximality and the high-link decompositions]\label{lem:r16maximal}
No new triple, including one with new points, can be added to $ R $.
Consequently every SF3 family of 17 triples is $\Pten\sqcup I_7$ or
$ P_9\sqcup I_8$, and every such family of 18 triples is
$\Pten\sqcup I_8$ or $ P_9\sqcup P_9$, on disjoint supports.
Here $ I_j $ denotes an intersecting SF3 family of size $ j $, and
$ P_9$ is $\Pten $ with one block removed.
The size 19 and 20 decompositions are respectively
$\Pten\sqcup P_9$ and $\Pten\sqcup\Pten $, again on disjoint supports.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Every hub has degree six and its complete SF2 link is already maximum.
A new triple avoids all hubs. Used pairs within $ D $ and within $ E $ have
codegree two, so it uses at most one point in each triad. A pair of $ D $
and a pair of $ E $ avoiding the new triple give two disjoint members of
$ R $, disjoint also from that triple. This is a forbidden empty sunflower.
If a family of 17--20 triples had at most seven disjoint triples per
root, every sixteen-member subfamily would be $ R $ and could not extend.
Thus some root has at least eight disjoint triples. B4 separates the
family into two intersecting parts of size at most ten. Their size pairs
are 10+7 or 9+8 at size 17,10+8 or 9+9 at size 18,10+9 at size 19,
and 10+10 at size 20. Isolation makes their
supports disjoint: a missing block of a P9 belongs to the same
disjointness class as that P9 and cannot be inserted in the other part.
\end{proof}
